data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Texts can carry one or several central ideas. This unit practices tracing how those ideas develop across paragraphs.

1. Read **More Than One Thread** — it upgrades everything you already knew.
2. Learn the terms in the **Glossary**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Word Scramble**.
3. Keep the **Evidence Moves** chart open while you work.
4. Sort the statements in **Claim, Evidence, or Neither?**
5. Take the quiz — it uses invented practice passages and asks you to CITE, not just pick.
6. Build an argument with the **Sentence Frames**.
7. Read the FAQ if you are curious how this works on things designed to persuade you.
8. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Evidence Moves** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
9. Finish with **Investigation: Fact-Check One Persuasive Text** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

The upgrade this year: never say 'the text says' without pointing to WHERE. Evidence has an address. 🔎

Picture panels: Trace the text; Locate and interpret evidence; Separate context from support; Represent the source fairly. Pictures support interpretation of the editable lesson text; they are not standalone evidence or answer keys. Numerical records and named practice stories are fictional. Read each sort in its stated context. Educator review is pending.

Sort by the stated role in each fictional proposal. Evidence statements also make assertions; “unrelated” means unrelated to this specific claim, not useless in every context. The data are invented and do not prove causes.

history.title: More Than One Thread
history.data:
## More Than One Thread

A **central idea** is a main point developed in a text. A text may have one or several central ideas. Length alone does not decide the number. An idea may be stated directly or **inferred** from details and their relationships.

To trace **development**, ask what each part adds. Does it introduce an idea, illustrate it, complicate it or qualify it? Do not just repeat the topic word beside every paragraph.

### Practice passage: The River Project
*The following four paragraphs are invented for this lesson. They are not a report of a real environmental study.*

**Paragraph 1.** Neighbors began collecting litter along a stream. At first, they chose dates informally, and several planned cleanups had too few helpers.

**Paragraph 2.** The group created a shared schedule and divided the work into short shifts. “A clear schedule helped us share the work,” one organizer wrote.

**Paragraph 3.** Volunteers counted filled litter bags and recorded the locations visited. Their notebook showed what had been collected, but the group had not measured the stream's chemical or biological condition.

**Paragraph 4.** The group kept its shared schedule and began asking a local science club how to collect more useful measurements. Members said that visible improvement was encouraging, but it was not enough to establish the stream's overall health.

One central idea is that organizing shared work can help a community project continue. Paragraph 1 introduces an attendance problem; paragraph 2 describes the schedule; paragraph 4 shows the group retaining it. Another is that evaluating results requires evidence suited to the question. Paragraphs 3 and 4 distinguish litter records from broader water-health measurements. The two ideas connect without saying the same thing.

A **claim** is a statement put forward for acceptance. **Evidence** is information offered as support, not automatically conclusive proof. **Reasoning** explains the connection and its limits. An unsupported claim might be true, false or uncertain; lacking support does not make it merely a preference.

To **cite**, identify the source and location. You may quote exact words or paraphrase accurately, following the task's instructions. For example: In paragraph 2, the organizer writes, “A clear schedule helped us share the work.” This supports the idea that coordination helped the project. The explanation is useful alongside the citation; it is not the citation itself. Litter records alone do not prove that water is safe or reveal what caused every change.

A detail can be related to the topic without being **relevant** to a particular claim. A stream's length might matter for planning how many helpers are needed, yet say little about whether the water condition improved.

An **objective** summary presents the text's important ideas fairly without personal evaluation. A **bias** can shape wording or selection; even accurate facts can be selected misleadingly. Persuasive writing can also be fair and well-supported. Ask what is offered, whether it supports the claim, and what remains uncertain instead of assuming deception.

All numerical examples in this pack are fictional practice data. A statistic written confidently is still something to verify in real research.

history.title: Cite It or Lose It

questions.question: What does tracing central-idea development require?
options: Explain how details introduce, extend or qualify one or more central ideas
Assume every text contains exactly two ideas
Stop using evidence in longer texts
Copy the first sentence of every paragraph
questions.correctAnswer: Explain how details introduce, extend or qualify one or more central ideas

questions.question: How do a main claim and its evidence relate in an argument?
options: A claim is always false
The claim states what is put forward; evidence is information offered to support it
Evidence is always conclusive proof
Only numbers can count as evidence
questions.correctAnswer: The claim states what is put forward; evidence is information offered to support it

questions.question: In The River Project, which detail most directly supports the idea that organizing helped shared work?
options: The project involved a stream
The organizer says in paragraph 2, “A clear schedule helped us share the work”
The group had not measured biological conditions
A stream has banks
questions.correctAnswer: The organizer says in paragraph 2, “A clear schedule helped us share the work”

questions.question: For the claim that an added library session attracted visits, which fictional detail is least relevant?
options: A log records 24 visits during that session
A log records 18 visits after the former closing time
A dated attendance sheet covers the trial session
The building was repainted last spring
questions.correctAnswer: The building was repainted last spring

questions.question: Which response uses an accurate quotation and explains its relevance to The River Project?
options: The project obviously worked in every way
Paragraph 2 says, “A clear schedule helped us share the work”; this supports the idea that coordination helped
Everyone knows schedules guarantee success
The river became safe, although the passage gives no measurements
questions.correctAnswer: Paragraph 2 says, “A clear schedule helped us share the work”; this supports the idea that coordination helped

questions.question: State the second central idea in The River Project and cite details from paragraphs 3 and 4 showing its development.
questions.expectedAnswer: A supported idea is that evaluating a project requires evidence suited to the question. Paragraph 3 explains that bag counts do not measure chemical or biological condition. Paragraph 4 adds the plan to seek better measurements and the limit of visible improvement. These details develop the distinction between collecting litter and establishing overall stream health. Faithful paraphrases with locations or accurate quotations are acceptable.

questions.question: The reading says 'relevance is not the same as relatedness.' Explain the difference and give your own example of a true but irrelevant detail.
questions.expectedAnswer: A detail can be about the same topic yet not support the particular claim. For a claim that 'the new bus route saves students time,' the detail 'the buses are yellow' is related to buses but does not support the claim about time. Relevant evidence would be actual travel-time data.

reflections.text: Think of an advertisement you have seen. What was its claim, and what evidence (if any) did it actually offer?
When is it hardest for you to find evidence in a text: long passages, or ideas that are only implied? Why?

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Analyst |
|---|---|---|---|
| Central idea | Gives a topic word | A central-idea sentence | Identifies a central idea AND how it develops |
| Evidence | No citation | Quotes once, no location | Cites 2+ times with location and exact words |
| Reasoning | Restates the quote | Links evidence to claim once | Explains each link AND tests relevance |

history.meta: 6 frames • rubric • two citations required at level 5

data.question: Can a text really have two main ideas without contradicting itself? 🤔
data.answer: Yes. A text can develop distinct but connected ideas, such as how people organize work and how they evaluate results. Their number must be established from the text, not assumed from its length.

data.question: What is the difference between evidence and just an opinion?
data.answer: Evidence is information offered as support. Opinions are judgments or beliefs and can also be claims. A ranking statistic can support a popularity claim, but does not by itself settle artistic quality.

data.question: Why do teachers care so much about citing WHERE? 📍
data.answer: A source and location let another reader check the wording, context and reasoning. Finding a line does not by itself establish that your interpretation is sound.

data.question: How does this help me with ads and social media?
data.answer: Look for claims, supporting information and missing context. Some persuasive writing is fair; evaluate specific wording and sources rather than assuming every writer is hiding facts.

data.question: What if the central idea is never actually stated?
data.answer: Infer it from details and relationships, then explain the evidence. Your interpretation should remain open to revision as you read further.

data.question: Is it cheating to quote the text instead of using my own words? ✍️
data.answer: Use quotation marks for exact borrowed words and cite the source. A faithful paraphrase also needs citation. Add your explanation of relevance; follow any instruction requiring direct quotations.

history.title: Investigation: Fact-Check One Persuasive Text
history.meta: 7th Grade • Investigation brief • trace the claims and grade the evidence

data.title: Fact-Check One Persuasive Text
data.instructions: Choose one teacher-approved public persuasive text. Trace its central ideas, list its main claims, evaluate offered support, and distinguish verified omissions from unanswered questions.
data.fitReason: The reading ends by saying the detective questions protect you far beyond any test. An investigation of a real persuasive text is where those questions do their job.

brief.context: Your class is building a 'Read It Like a Detective' guide for sixth graders. Each team takes one persuasive text aimed at kids or teens: a snack ad, a sneaker commercial, an app's 'why you need this' page, or an opinion piece from a student newspaper.
brief.audience: Sixth graders who will use your guide, and the teacher who checks your citations
brief.drivingQuestion: What does this text want us to accept, what evidence does it actually offer for each claim, how relevant is that evidence, and what has been left out?
brief.seedDirection: List the claims before you judge anything. You cannot grade evidence for a claim you have not written down.
lockedLessonFacts: A text may have one or several central ideas.
Evidence is information offered as support, not automatic proof.
Cite sources, represent them accurately, and explain relevance.
Evaluate persuasive writing fairly; loaded language or omissions require specific evidence.
A missing piece may be an unanswered question rather than a fact you can assume.
openQuestions: Who made this text, and what do they gain if we accept it?
Which sentences are claims and which are evidence?
For each piece of evidence, could it be checked by someone else?
What fact would weaken the text's case, and is it anywhere in the text?
stakeholders: The company or writer who made the text
Teachers who may use the guide
criteria: Every claim is quoted with its location
Every piece of evidence is graded relevant, related-only, or missing, with a reason
At least one central idea is traced from beginning to end of the text
Identify relevant missing information if present, or explain what remains uncertain; do not invent an omission
Uses at least four glossary words correctly
constraints: Texts must be public and made for a general audience; no private messages
Be fair: quote exactly and do not exaggerate what the text says
Two pages including the claim table
brief.deliverable: A claim-and-evidence table (claim, location, evidence, grade, reason), a paragraph tracing one central idea, and a short 'what it leaves out' section, written so a sixth grader can follow it.

parallelExample.context: Invented example: a student reviews a public poster asking for longer library hours.
parallelExample.move: The poster cites after-school visits but gives no staffing estimate. The student checks the cited attendance record and marks future staffing cost as missing information, without claiming the author intentionally hid it.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: The analysis identifies a claim, checks offered support and separates a real gap from a guess about motive.

supports.frameStarter: The text claims ____ (location: ____). Its evidence is '____.' This evidence is ____ because ____. It leaves out ____.
frameChoices: Grade each piece of evidence as relevant, related-only, or missing
Trace how one central idea develops from the first line to the last
Compare what the text says with one fact from a source it does not mention
Rewrite one claim as a fair version with the evidence it would need
coachPrompts: Which claim in your table has the weakest evidence, and does the text make it sound the strongest?
Where does loaded language do the work that evidence should do?
Could a sixth grader check any of the evidence on their own?

data.coachHint: Claims first, in their own words and yours. Then evidence. Then relevance. Then the missing piece. Do not skip the order.
